This proves that the probability of the specified endpoint list together with all its good events is at most $$(1+n^{-2})^{n-n/8}\frac{(n/8)!}{n!}
 \le2\frac{|H_i|}{|G|}.$$ The subprobability $f$ also requires the other orders’ good events, so it is bounded by this probability. A coset $gH_i$ specifies exactly this complement endpoint list, proving <a href="#noise:predictable-cap" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="noise:predictable-cap">[noise:predictable-cap]</a>. ◻

</details>

<a id="pm-h-18"></a>
#### The four corresponding full-permutation applications

The information just obtained has three different forms: a uniform list estimate, an average over lists, and one subprobability with predictable pointwise caps. They enter distinct Fourier arguments. The statements below preserve the quantitative conclusions of those arguments; all times count physical shuffles.

<a id="stmt-noise-mixing"></a>
<div id="noise:mixing" class="theorem">

**Theorem 14**. *For the Thorp shuffle on $n=2^d$, each of the following methods proves worst-start total-variation convergence to uniform at the indicated time:*

1.  *the sixteen-subgroup orbit-span argument at $8192d$;*

2.  *predictable coset caps at $16384d$;*

3.  *diagram peeling at $400\cdot2^{22}d$;*

4.  *the covariance and four-subgroup coefficient argument at $16000d$.*

*The $2048d$ fixed-list and isotypic route was completed in Section <a href="#sec:first-route" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:first-route">3</a>.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-noise-mixing"><summary>Proof of stmt-noise-mixing</summary>

*Proof.* Write $C_u=\sup_{m\ge1}\sum_{\tau\vdash m}D_\tau^{-u}$ for the finite constants proved in <a id="pm-cite-22"></a>[[partialFourier](#ref-partialFourier), Theorem l-l:degree-all-powers]. For the separate peeling argument put $C_{\rm peel}=512^2$. As before, every untrimmed positive-time shuffle block has zero sign expectation. All the lifting statements invoked below are proved independently in <a id="pm-cite-23"></a>[[partialFourier](#ref-partialFourier)].

For the $1024d$ law, apply the first part of Proposition <a href="#noise:uniform-marginals" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="noise:uniform-marginals">7</a> with $b=16$ blocks. Use the sequential trimming operation in Lemma [l-l:trim] of <a id="pm-cite-24"></a>[[partialFourier](#ref-partialFourier)]: reduce each coset mass exceeding its uniform mass to that mass. Each reduction preserves the earlier caps, and the total mass removed is at most $\varepsilon=bn^{-3/2}$. The resulting subprobability $f\le\mu$ has mass $z\ge1-\varepsilon$ and caps one. Thus $\nu=f/z$ satisfies $\|\nu-\mu\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\le\varepsilon$ and has cap two when $\varepsilon\le1/2$. Proposition [l-l:orbit-span] of <a id="pm-cite-25"></a>[[partialFourier](#ref-partialFourier)] bounds the operator norm by $A D^{-3/8}$, $A=\sqrt{2bC_2}$. Since $\|B^8\|_{\mathrm{HS}}\le\sqrt D\|B\|_{\mathrm{op}}^8$, the nonsign sum is at most $A^{16}\sum_{D>1}D^{2-6}=o(1)$. Its sign coefficient has absolute value at most $2bn^{-3/2}$. The same probability comparison proves mixing at $8\cdot1024d$.

<a id="noise:subprob-plancherel"></a>
For the predictable construction, let $f\le\mu$ be supplied by Proposition <a href="#noise:predictable-cosets" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="noise:predictable-cosets">13</a>, and put $z=\sum f$. Proposition [l-l:isotypic] of <a id="pm-cite-26"></a>[[partialFourier](#ref-partialFourier)], with $B=2,b=8$, gives $\|\widehat f(\rho)\|_{\mathrm{HS}}^2\le16C_2D^{-1/2}$. Eight powers again leave an inverse-cube dimension sum. Its sign coefficient is bounded by $1-z=o(1)$ and its trivial coefficient is $z$. More explicitly, for any fixed $R$, $$\|f^{*R}-z^R U_G\|_1^2
 \le\sum_{\rho\ne\mathrm{triv}}
 D_\rho\|\widehat f(\rho)^R\|_{\mathrm{HS}}^2.
 \label{noise:subprob-plancherel}$$ Thus the right side tends to zero for $R=8$. The differences $\mu^{*R}-f^{*R}$ and $U_G-z^RU_G$ have $\ell^1$ norms $1-z^R=o(1)$, since the former is nonnegative. This proves mixing after $8\cdot2048d$.

For peeling, take $b=2^{22}$ and $T=100bd$ in Proposition <a href="#noise:averaged-general" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="noise:averaged-general">11</a>. A uniform equal-size partition has uniformly distributed complements, so averaging selects one deterministic partition whose sum of complement errors is $o(1)$. Heavy-coset deletion gives a subprobability $\eta\le\mu$ of mass $1-o(1)$ and cap two. Since $b\ge4(C_{\rm peel}+2)$, Corollary [l-l:peeling-lift] of <a id="pm-cite-27"></a>[[partialFourier](#ref-partialFourier)] implies $$\sum_{D_\rho>1}D_\rho\|\widehat\eta(\rho)^4\|_{\mathrm{HS}}^2
 \le(6b)^4\sum_{D_\rho>1}
 D_\rho^{1-4(1-(C_{\rm peel}+2)/b)}=o(1),$$ because the exponent is at most $-2$ and Theorem [l-l:degree-all-powers] of <a id="pm-cite-28"></a>[[partialFourier](#ref-partialFourier)] applies. The trivial and sign coefficients, and restoration of missing mass, are handled exactly by <a href="#noise:subprob-plancherel" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="noise:subprob-plancherel">[noise:subprob-plancherel]</a>. The total physical time is $4T=400\cdot2^{22}d$.

Finally, Proposition <a href="#noise:covariance-marginal" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="noise:covariance-marginal">12</a> selects, by the same averaging argument, a deterministic partition into four blocks with complement errors summing to $o(1)$ for the $1000d$ law. Trim to a subprobability $\eta$ of mass $1-o(1)$ and cap two. Proposition [l-l:four-coefficient] of <a id="pm-cite-29"></a>[[partialFourier](#ref-partialFourier)] gives $\|\widehat\eta(\rho)\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le C D^{-1/8}$. After sixteen factors the nontrivial nonsign sum is at most $$C^{32}\sum_{\rho\ne\mathrm{triv},\mathop{\mathrm{sgn}}}D^{2-16/4}
 =C^{32}\sum_{\rho\ne\mathrm{triv},\mathop{\mathrm{sgn}}}D^{-2}=o(1).$$ Again parity and missing mass are controlled as above. This proves the covariance route at $16\cdot1000d=16000d$.

All blocks contain a whole number of sweeps. The moving frame therefore returns to the physical coordinates, and independent blocks have the convolution laws used above. Equation <a href="#eq:worst-state" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:worst-state">[eq:worst-state]</a> supplies worst-start uniformity in every case. The lower obstruction is <a href="#eq:support" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:support">[eq:support]</a>; it is independent of which upper-bound method is used. ◻

</details>

<a id="mart:section"></a>
### Fixed domains, random domains, and Walsh coordinates

The finite-memory weights admit a second explanation: count the Walsh characters whose last active coordinate was updated at each preceding layer. We give that derivation first, then compare two ways of obtaining the opposite-half balance used in Section <a href="#sec:first-route" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:first-route">3</a>. A fixed domain acquires balance from the preceding switch layer; a random domain also has balance by sampling without replacement. The resulting table records the quantitative inputs used by several distinct Fourier transfers. Random sampling is needed for the smaller-subcube argument of Section <a href="#sec:noise-extensions" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:noise-extensions">5</a>, but it is not needed to obtain the half-density bounds in this section.

We retain $V=\{0,1\}^d$, $n=2^d$, and $G=\mathop{\mathrm{Sym}}(V)$. In the cyclic coordinate frame, layer $s$ uses $i_s=1+(s\bmod d)$. The position permutation in that frame is $\Pi_s$. A sweep consists of $d$ layers; at every sweep boundary the frame is the physical position frame.

<a id="mart:flow-section"></a>
#### Walsh coordinates of the adapted flow

Fix an ordered list $(x_1,\ldots,x_k)$ of distinct input positions and expose the paths of its first $\ell$ cards. The list may be deterministic or sampled independently of the shuffle. The next card is the tagged card. Let $\mathcal F_s$ contain the list and the exposed paths through time $s$, and let $V_s$ be the set of positions not occupied by exposed cards. Its size is $m=n-\ell$. Given a terminal time $T$, define $$p_s(x)=\mathbb P(\Pi_s(x_{\ell+1})=x\mid\mathcal F_T),\qquad
 f_s=p_s-m^{-1}\mathbf1_{V_s}\quad(0\le s\le T).$$ These are the available set and centered vector of Section <a href="#sec:first-route" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:first-route">3</a>. Lemma <a href="#lem:marginal-averaging" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:marginal-averaging">2</a> applies with the exposed cards as blockers: although $p_s$ conditions on complete paths, it has an $\mathcal F_s$-measurable version. Thus $f_s$ has sum zero, is supported on $V_s$, and has squared norm at most one.

Use the coordinate average $P_i$ from Section <a href="#sec:first-route" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:first-route">3</a>, and write $x^{(i)}=x\oplus e_i$ for the partner of $x$. In the following expectations we sample the shuffle and, when applicable, the initial list; we do not fix its terminal exposed paths. Set $$a_s=\mathbb E\|f_s\|_2^2,\qquad
 L_s=\sum_x f_s(x)^2\mathbf1_{\{x^{(i_s)}\notin V_s\}},
 \qquad w_s=\mathbb E L_s.$$

<a id="mart:energy"></a>
With this notation, Lemma <a href="#noise:memory" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="noise:memory">5</a> reads <a id="mart:noise-update"></a>$$\label{mart:noise-update}
 f_{s+1}=P_{i_s}f_s+\xi_s,\qquad
 \mathbb E(\xi_s\mid\mathcal F_s)=0.$$ On each edge with exactly one available position $x$, its noise is $\pm f_s(x)(\delta_x-\delta_{x^{(i_s)}})/2$, with independent fair signs on distinct such edges. All other edges contribute zero noise. For every $t\ge d$, $$\label{mart:energy}
 a_t=\sum_{j=1}^d2^{-j}w_{t-j}.$$ Equivalently, with $D_s=\mathbb E\|\xi_s\|_2^2=w_s/2$, $a_t=\sum_{j=1}^d2^{-(j-1)}D_{t-j}$. There is also a coordinate-frequency proof, using the finite Boolean version of the Walsh character basis <a id="pm-cite-30"></a>[[walsh1923](#ref-walsh1923)]. It avoids expanding the vector recursion and identifies the same weights by counting the last update of each character.

<a id="stmt-mart-walsh"></a>
<div id="mart:walsh" class="lemma">

**Lemma 15** (Walsh derivation). *For $A\subseteq\{1,\ldots,d\}$, define $\widehat f_s(A)=\sum_xf_s(x)(-1)^{\sum_{i\in A}x_i}$. If $i_s\notin A$, then $\widehat f_{s+1}(A)=\widehat f_s(A)$. If $i_s\in A$, then <a id="mart:walsh-update"></a>$$\label{mart:walsh-update}
 \mathbb E\bigl(\widehat f_{s+1}(A)^2\mid\mathcal F_s\bigr)=L_s.$$ These identities imply <a href="#mart:energy" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="mart:energy">[mart:energy]</a>.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-mart-walsh"><summary>Proof of stmt-mart-walsh</summary>

*Proof.* A character omitting the active coordinate is constant on every updated edge, and the update preserves the sum on that edge. A character containing the active coordinate has opposite values at the endpoints. An edge with two available positions contributes zero after averaging. Each edge with one available position contributes its entry times an independent centered sign. The conditional second moment is therefore $L_s$.

At time $t\ge d$, every nonempty character has a last update among the previous $d$ layers. Exactly $2^{d-j}$ subsets have their last update at time $t-j$: they include that coordinate, omit the $j-1$ more recent coordinates, and choose arbitrarily among the other $d-j$. The empty coefficient is zero. Parseval, with normalization $\|f\|_2^2=n^{-1}\sum_A\widehat f(A)^2$, now gives <a href="#mart:energy" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="mart:energy">[mart:energy]</a>. ◻

</details>

<a id="mart:balance-section"></a>
#### Opposite halves and large marginals

The remaining input to the scalar recurrence is a gain when an available position meets another available position. The masses and the available set are generally correlated. The needed independence holds across the two halves during the $d-1$ intervening coordinate updates.

<a id="stmt-mart-halves"></a>
<div id="mart:halves" class="lemma">

<a id="mart:half-factorization"></a>
<a id="mart:noise-bound"></a>
**Lemma 16** (Half-space factorization). *Fix $s\ge d-1$, put $a=s-d+1$, and let $H_0,H_1$ be the two halves defined by coordinate $i_s$. Conditional on $\mathcal F_a$, for $h\in\{0,1\}$, $$\label{mart:half-factorization}
 \mathbb E\!\left[
  \sum_{x\in H_h}f_s(x)^2\mathbf1_{\{x^{(i_s)}\in V_s\}}
       \,\middle|\,\mathcal F_a\right]
 =\frac{|V_a\cap H_{1-h}|}{n/2}
   \mathbb E\!\left[\sum_{x\in H_h}f_s(x)^2
       \,\middle|\,\mathcal F_a\right].$$ If both half densities at time $a$ are at least $\beta$ except on an $\mathcal F_a$-measurable event of probability at most $\eta$, then $$\label{mart:noise-bound}
 w_s\le(1-\beta)a_s+\eta.$$*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-mart-halves"><summary>Proof of stmt-mart-halves</summary>

*Proof.* The updates from $a$ through $s-1$ visit each coordinate other than $i_s$ once and never cross the two halves. Given the initial history, the future switch arrays in the halves are independent of that history and of each other. Starting from the now known restrictions of $V_a$ and $f_a$, both the exposed paths and the forward flow inside one half are measurable functions of that half’s switch array alone. The cylinder description in Lemma <a href="#lem:marginal-averaging" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:marginal-averaging">2</a> leaves its unvisited switches independent, so computing the conditional flow introduces no dependence on the other half. The flow value at $x$ uses only the array in its own half, whereas the opposite partner’s membership in $V_s$ uses the other array. In that other half, each exposed card is marginally uniform after these $d-1$ layers, since each remaining bit has been refreshed with a fair bit. Distinctness of the card positions gives the stated expected available density. This proves <a href="#mart:half-factorization" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="mart:half-factorization">[mart:half-factorization]</a>. Subtract the available-partner contribution from $a_s$ and use $\|f_s\|_2^2\le1$ on the exceptional event to obtain <a href="#mart:noise-bound" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="mart:noise-bound">[mart:noise-bound]</a>. ◻

</details>

We record the two sources of balance, as they yield different uniformity statements about the initial domain.

<a id="stmt-mart-balance"></a>
<div id="mart:balance" class="lemma">

**Lemma 17** (Fixed and random initial domains). *Suppose $m\ge n/q$, where $q\ge1$ is a fixed integer.*

1.  *For every deterministic initial list, <a href="#mart:noise-bound" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="mart:noise-bound">[mart:noise-bound]</a> holds for $s\ge d$ with $\beta=1/(2q)$ and $\eta=2\exp(-n/(8q))$.*

2.  *If the initial list is uniformly random and independent of the shuffle, it holds for $s\ge d-1$ with $\beta=1/(2q)$ and either of the valid bounds $$\eta=2\exp(-n/(32q)),\qquad
     \eta=2(n+1)\exp\!\left(-\frac{(1-\log2)n}{4q}\right).$$*

3.  *In the random-list setting it also holds with $\beta=1/(4q)$ and $\eta=2\exp(-c n/q)$ for an absolute $c>0$, using the weaker requirement $|V_a\cap H_h|\ge m/8$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-mart-balance"><summary>Proof of stmt-mart-balance</summary>

*Proof.* For the first assertion, $a=s-d+1\ge1$ is the time immediately after the preceding update in coordinate $i_s$. Given the history before that update, either half’s available count is $A+\operatorname{Bin}(L,1/2)$, where $2A+L=m$ and $L\le m$. A deviation below $m/4$ has probability at most $\exp(-m/8)$ by the independent bounded-difference estimate for the $L$ fair choices. The union bound handles both halves. Each half with at least $m/4$ available positions has available density at least $1/(2q)$.

For a random list, $V_a$ is unconditionally a uniform $m$-subset, because a fixed permutation maps a uniform subset to a uniform subset. This statement is unconditional; no independence of $f_a$ and $V_a$ is asserted. A half count has mean $m/2$. Its Doob martingale under sequential sampling without replacement has increments of absolute value at most one: changing the next draw can be coupled with the remaining completion by exchanging those two sites. The bounded-increment martingale inequality gives probability at most $\exp(-m/32)$ for a downward deviation of $m/4$, proving the first displayed choice.

For the other choice, sample independent Bernoulli variables with parameter $m/n$ and condition their total to equal $m$. The latter event has probability at least $1/(n+1)$ since $m$ is a binomial mode; the case $m=n$ is deterministic. Before conditioning, a half count $X$ satisfies $\mathbb E2^{-X}\le e^{-m/4}$. Thus $\mathbb P(X<m/4)\le\exp(-(1-\log2)m/4)$. Condition and sum over the two halves.

Finally, failure of the $m/8$ balance forces at least $k=\lceil7m/8\rceil$ of the $m$ sampled sites into one half. For any specified $k$ sample indices the probability is at most $2^{-k}$. The union bound gives $2\binom mk2^{-k}$, which is at most $2e^{-cm}$: use $\binom m{m-k}\le(8e)^{m/8}$ and $(7/8)\log2-(1/8)\log(8e)>0$. Lemma <a href="#mart:halves" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="mart:halves">16</a> now proves all three assertions. ◻

</details>

<a id="stmt-mart-decay"></a>
<div id="mart:decay" class="lemma">

**Lemma 18** (Scalar decay and sequential comparison). *If <a href="#mart:noise-bound" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="mart:noise-bound">[mart:noise-bound]</a> holds for every $s\ge d$, then for any $\gamma\in[1-\beta/2,1)$, <a id="mart:decay-bound"></a>$$\label{mart:decay-bound}
 a_t\le\gamma^{t-2d}+\eta/\beta\qquad(t\ge0).$$ At time $T$, the total-variation distance of the images of a list of $k$ cards from the uniform injection is at most the sum of the expected conditional tagged distances. Each such summand is at most $\frac12\sqrt{ma_T}\le\frac12\sqrt{na_T}$. The estimates hold for each deterministic list under the first balance assertion, and on average over lists under the other assertions.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-mart-decay"><summary>Proof of stmt-mart-decay</summary>

*Proof.* Apply <a href="#noise:comparison-solution" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="noise:comparison-solution">[noise:comparison-solution]</a> with $\rho=1-\beta$, $s_0=d$, $t_0=2d$, and $a_0\le1$. The condition on $\gamma$ is exactly $(1-\beta)/(2\gamma-1)\le1$. For each list entry, Cauchy–Schwarz bounds the mean path-conditioned variation by $\frac12\mathbb E\|f_T\|_1\le\frac12\sqrt{ma_T}$. Lemma <a href="#lem:sequential-tv" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:sequential-tv">[lem:sequential-tv]</a> sums these errors: its uniform reference depends only on the previously exposed endpoints, so its path-conditioning version applies. Averaging this inequality over an independently sampled list gives the random-domain assertion. ◻

</details>

<a id="stmt-mart-marginals"></a>
<div id="mart:marginals" class="proposition">

**Proposition 19** (Quantitative marginal estimates). *The following choices give the indicated energy bounds uniformly over the sequential indices, and hence the corresponding large-marginal estimates. In each row $q$ is fixed and at most $n-n/q$ cards are observed. The letters $C_{\mathrm{fix}},L,C,b_0$ denote fixed integers satisfying the displayed conditions.*

<div class="center">

| *Input used* |   *$q$*    | *$\beta$*  |  *$\gamma$*   |            *Time and energy*             |
|:------------:|:----------:|:----------:|:-------------:|:----------------------------------------:|
|   *fixed*    |   *$16$*   |  *$1/32$*  |  *$127/128$*  | *$T=C_{\mathrm{fix}}d$, $a_T=O(n^{-6})$* |
|   *fixed*    |   *$8$*    |  *$1/16$*  |   *$63/64$*   |       *$T=512d$, $a_T=O(n^{-7})$*        |
|   *random*   |   *$32$*   |  *$1/64$*  |  *$127/128$*  |        *$T=Ld$, $a_T=O(n^{-10})$*        |
|   *random*   |   *$8$*    |  *$1/16$*  |   *$31/32$*   |       *$T=200d$, $a_T=O(n^{-8})$*        |
|   *random*   |  *$256$*   | *$1/1024$* | *$2047/2048$* |        *$T=Cd$, $a_T=o(n^{-4})$*         |
|   *random*   |   *$64$*   | *$1/128$*  |  *$511/512$*  |       *$T=b_0d$, $a_T=O(n^{-5})$*        |
|   *random*   | *$K=8192$* | *$1/(2K)$* | *$1-1/(8K)$*  |     *$T=(100K+2)d$, $a_T=o(n^{-4})$*     |

</div>

*The integer choices are $$(127/128)^{C_{\mathrm{fix}}-2}\le2^{-6},\quad
 (127/128)^{L-2}\le2^{-10},\quad
 (2047/2048)^{C-2}<2^{-4},\quad
 (511/512)^{b_0-2}\le2^{-5}.$$ The first two rows will be used for prescribed lists, and the other rows on average over uniform initial lists. In fact the fixed-domain part of Lemma <a href="#mart:balance" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="mart:balance">17</a> also proves every energy bound in the table for each prescribed list: it has at least the displayed $\beta$ and an exponentially small exceptional term. The distinction in the table records the information used by the transfers below. In particular the eight-block random-domain row has average marginal distance $O(n^{-5/2})$, and the $64$-block row has distance $O(n^{-1})$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-mart-marginals"><summary>Proof of stmt-mart-marginals</summary>

*Proof.* Apply Lemmas <a href="#mart:balance" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="mart:balance">17</a> and <a href="#mart:decay" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="mart:decay">18</a>. The $256$-block row uses the $m/8$ threshold; the other rows use $m/4$. The exceptional terms are exponentially small in $n$. For the numerical choices, $(63/64)^{510d}=O(2^{-7d})$ and $(31/32)^{198d}\le2^{-8d}$, since $198\log_2(32/31)>8$. In the last row the geometric term is at most $\exp(-100d/8)=o(2^{-4d})$. The sequential estimate multiplies $\sqrt{na_T}/2$ by at most $n$, giving the claimed errors. ◻

</details>

<a id="mart:applications"></a>
#### Using the marginal bounds on the full permutation group

We now specify how each row of Proposition <a href="#mart:marginals" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="mart:marginals">19</a> supplies a full-deck bound. This passage uses the abstract results of *From partial permutation information to Fourier bounds <a id="pm-cite-31"></a>[[partialFourier](#ref-partialFourier)]* . We state the needed bounds at their point of use. They use the mass transform $\widehat\nu(\rho)=\sum_{g\in G}\nu(g)\rho(g)$ and unnormalized Hilbert–Schmidt norm. For $u>0$, put $C_u=\sup_{m\ge1}\sum_{\tau\in\widehat{S_m}}(\dim\tau)^{-u}$. Theorem [l-l:degree-all-powers] of <a id="pm-cite-32"></a>[[partialFourier](#ref-partialFourier)] gives $C_u<\infty$ and $\sum_{\rho\ne\mathbf1,\mathop{\mathrm{sgn}}}(\dim\rho)^{-u}=o(1)$ as $n\to\infty$.

For a partition into $q$ equal blocks, retain the subgroups $H_i=\mathop{\mathrm{Sym}}(D_i)$ and left-coset convention of Section <a href="#sec:probability-completion" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:probability-completion">3.3</a>. A fixed-list bound supplies every such partition; an averaged bound supplies one by averaging the sum of its $q$ complementary marginal errors. In either case write that sum as $\delta_n=o(1)$.

We use the common trimming operations from <a id="pm-cite-33"></a>[[partialFourier](#ref-partialFourier), Lemma l-l:trim]. Heavy-coset deletion and normalization give a probability within $o(1)$ of the block law, with cap $B/[G:H_i]$ for $B=3$ or $4$. Successive excess trimming instead gives a subprobability of mass at least $1-\delta_n$ and cap one. Heavy-coset deletion without normalization gives mass $1-o(1)$ and cap two. Each operation produces one measure satisfying all the caps simultaneously.

<a id="stmt-mart-application-times"></a>
<div id="mart:application-times" class="proposition">

**Proposition 20** (Quantitative applications of the martingale bounds). *Use the integer parameters specified in Proposition <a href="#mart:marginals" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="mart:marginals">19</a>. Every total time in Table <a href="#mart:transfer-table" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="mart:transfer-table">1</a> gives worst-start total-variation convergence to uniform as $d\to\infty$.*

</div>

<a id="mart:hs16"></a>
<a id="mart:hs8"></a>
<a id="mart:hs64"></a>
The table distinguishes a bound on the operator norm from one on the *squared*, unnormalized Hilbert–Schmidt norm. For its first three rows using squared Hilbert–Schmidt bounds, the exact inequalities are $$\begin{aligned}
 D\|\widehat\nu(\rho)\|_{\mathrm{HS}}^2
 &\le9qC_2D^{4/q} &&(q=16,\ B=3),\label{mart:hs16}\\
 \|\widehat\nu(\rho)\|_{\mathrm{HS}}^2
 &\le qC_2D^{-1+6/q} &&(q=8,\ B=1),\label{mart:hs8}\\
 \|\widehat\nu(\rho)\|_{\mathrm{HS}}^2
 &\le4qC_{16}D^{-1+18/q} &&(q=64,\ B=4).\label{mart:hs64}
\end{aligned}$$ Here $\nu$ denotes the retained measure specified in the corresponding row, and $D=\dim\rho$. The constants in the other rows are also independent of $n$, except for $M=1-o(1)$, the retained probability in the random-partition construction.

<div id="mart:transfer-table">

| Transfer and retained law                                          | Fourier bound                                                                                           |  $r$ | $\kappa$ |      Total time$/d$ |
|:-------------------------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-----:|---------:|--------------------:|
| Transfer and retained law                                          | Fourier bound                                                                                           |  $r$ | $\kappa$ |      Total time$/d$ |
| Random partition, $q=8$; probability, mass $M$ before conditioning | $\mathrm{op}:\ \dfrac2M\sqrt{16C_1}D^{-5/16}$                                                           |  $8$ |     $-3$ |              $1600$ |
| Coefficient space, $q=16$;probability, cap $3$                     | HS squared: <a href="#mart:hs16" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="mart:hs16">[mart:hs16]</a> |  $4$ |     $-2$ | $4C_{\mathrm{fix}}$ |
| Pointwise character, $q=8$;subprobability, cap $1$                 | HS squared: <a href="#mart:hs8" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="mart:hs8">[mart:hs8]</a>    | $16$ |     $-3$ |              $8192$ |
| Global isotypic, $q=64$;probability, cap $4$                       | HS squared: <a href="#mart:hs64" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="mart:hs64">[mart:hs64]</a> | $32$ |    $-22$ |             $32b_0$ |
| Coefficient average, $q=32$;probability, cap $4$                   | $\mathrm{op}:\ \dfrac83\sqrt{C_1}D^{-5/16}$                                                             |  $8$ |     $-3$ |                $8L$ |
| Orbit average, $q=256$;probability, cap $4$                        | $\mathrm{op}:\ 4\sqrt{C_{32}}D^{-1/4}$                                                                  | $72$ |    $-34$ |               $72C$ |
| Small-index character,$K=q=8192$;subprobability, cap $2$           | $\mathrm{HS}^2:\ 2KC_1D^{-1+1026/K}$                                                                    |  $4$ |  $\le-1$ |           $3276808$ |

Fourier substitutions for the marginal bounds. The column $r$ counts independent blocks; $\kappa$ bounds the exponent of $D$ in their nonsign Plancherel summand, up to a fixed factor.

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-mart-application-times"><summary>Proof of stmt-mart-application-times</summary>

*Proof.* All Fourier bounds in the table are exact cases of <a id="pm-cite-34"></a>[[partialFourier](#ref-partialFourier)]: Proposition [l-l:random-partition] for the first row; Proposition [l-l:coefficient-lift] for the coefficient and pointwise-character rows; Proposition [l-l:isotypic] for the global isotypic row; Propositions [l-l:coefficient-average] and [l-l:orbit-average] for the two projection averages; and Theorem [l-l:character-lift] for the last row. The last transfer uses a one-dimensional character of index at most $b^{1024}$ in every block type of degree $b$, which gives $(1024+2)/K=1026/8192<1/4$ in its displayed bound.

The first row uses the averaged complementary-coset estimate at $200d$ directly. Its transfer constructs a conditional probability law and keeps the partition random inside the coefficient estimate; it does not select a deterministic partition there. All other rows use the selected partition and the indicated common trimming.

For an operator bound $A D^{-\beta}$, the probability completion of Section <a href="#sec:probability-completion" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:probability-completion">3.3</a> gives a nonsign summand $A^{2r}D^{2-2r\beta}$. For a squared Hilbert–Schmidt bound $A D^{-\beta}$, it gives $A^rD^{1-r\beta}$. Substitution gives the column $\kappa$. Every displayed upper exponent is negative, so the corresponding reciprocal-degree sum tends to zero. In particular the pointwise-character and small-index rows use subprobabilities; they need the same norm calculation with their mass retained.

To finish those two rows, let $z=\nu(G)=1-o(1)$. Since the original shuffle block has zero sign expectation, the retained subprobability has sign coefficient at most $1-z$. Equation <a href="#noise:subprob-plancherel" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="noise:subprob-plancherel">[noise:subprob-plancherel]</a> makes $\|\nu^{*r}-z^rU_G\|_1=o(1)$, while restoring the missing mass costs $1-z^r\le r(1-z)$ in each of the two positive measures. For the probability rows, closeness to the original block law gives sign coefficient $o(1)$ and permits replacement of the $r$ factors, as in Section <a href="#sec:probability-completion" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:probability-completion">3.3</a>.

Finally multiply the corresponding block length from Proposition <a href="#mart:marginals" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="mart:marginals">19</a> by $r$. For the last row this is $4(100\cdot8192+2)d=3276808d$. All block lengths are multiples of $d$, so their convolutions are physical shuffle blocks. Translation by a deterministic starting deck preserves distance from uniform. ◻

</details>

<a id="cycles:section"></a>
### Conditional weights for the cyclic coordinate schedule

The deterministic coordinate schedule admits estimates that do not use an auxiliary change to random directions. We first give several two-sweep estimates for arbitrary initial available sets and signed weights. They yield uniform mixing of any prescribed list omitting a fixed positive fraction of the cards. We then track the bitwise difference of two conditional weights. This autocorrelation gives predictable marginal caps in both coordinate orders; a two-sided Fourier transfer turns those caps into a $2052d$ bound.

Throughout this section $n=2^d$, $V=\mathbb F_2^d$, and $G=\mathop{\mathrm{Sym}}(V)$. A *sweep* means the $d$ consecutive coordinate layers $1,\ldots,d$ in the rotating frame of <a href="#eq:frames:cyclic" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:frames:cyclic">[eq:frames:cyclic]</a>. At a sweep boundary this frame agrees with the physical position frame. The arguments also hold after any permutation of the coordinate order, including its reversal. All norms on real vectors on $V$ below use counting measure.

<a id="cycles:weights"></a>
#### Signed weights on the available set

<a id="cycles:mean-update"></a>
Let $F\subseteq V$ be a moving set of available positions and put $h=\mathbf 1_F$. Attach a real vector $f$ supported on $F$. A coordinate layer updates each matching pair as follows: with two available endpoints, replace their weights by their average; with one available endpoint, place its flag and weight at one of the two endpoints with equal probabilities; with no available endpoint, leave both weights zero. The choices on distinct pairs are independent. This preserves $|F|$ and $\sum_x f(x)$, and never increases $\|f\|_2^2$. Write $A_j$ for ordinary averaging across coordinate $j$, and $B_i=A_i\cdots A_1$, with $B_0=I$. Conditional on the past, $$\label{cycles:mean-update}
 \mathbb E(f_{\rm new}\mid h,f)=A_jf,\qquad
 \mathbb E(h_{\rm new}\mid h,f)=A_jh,\qquad
 \mathbb E(f_{\rm new}^2\mid h,f)\le A_j(f^2)$$ pointwise. The first two identities follow by inspecting the three pair types. For the last, two weights at available endpoints satisfy $((a+b)/2)^2\le(a^2+b^2)/2$, and the other cases are equalities.

<a id="cycles:conditional-weight"></a>
This process includes the centered conditional distribution of one card after the trajectories of several other cards have been exposed. Write $X_t(a)$ for the location of the card started at $a$ in the cyclic coordinate frame. More precisely, if $j$ cards are observed through time $t$, let $\mathcal F_t$ be their trajectory field, $F_t$ their complement, and $a$ a further initial label. Then $$\label{cycles:conditional-weight}
 f_t(x)=\Pr(X_t(a)=x\mid\mathcal F_t)
               -\frac{\mathbf 1_{F_t}(x)}{n-j}$$ has exactly the transition law above by Lemma <a href="#lem:marginal-averaging" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:marginal-averaging">2</a>, applied with the observed cards as blockers. The same rule transports the uniform vector on the available set. The process is adapted to $\mathcal F_t$; it is not obtained by conditioning its transitions on a future event. Its initial energy is at most one. The real weights considered here have broader scope than this application: they may be any deterministic signed vector supported on the initial available set. The contraction statements below retain that scope, with their stated zero-sum hypotheses.

<a id="stmt-cycles-list"></a>
<div id="cycles:list" class="lemma">

**Lemma 21** (From signed-weight energy to list mixing). *Fix $p\in(0,1)$ and an integer $R\ge1$. Suppose every deterministic zero-sum weight configuration on an available set with $|F|\ge pn$ satisfies $\mathbb E\|f_{2d}\|_2^2\le \kappa_d\|f_0\|_2^2$ over two sweeps. After $2R$ sweeps the images of any fixed ordered list of at most $(1-p)n$ distinct initial labels have total-variation distance at most <a id="cycles:list-error"></a>$$\label{cycles:list-error}
 \frac12 n^{3/2}\kappa_d^{R/2}$$ from the uniform distinct-position list.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-cycles-list"><summary>Proof of stmt-cycles-list</summary>

*Proof.* Successive conditioning at two-sweep boundaries gives $\mathbb E\|f_{2Rd}\|_2^2\le \kappa_d^R$ for the centered conditional law of each next card, exposing all preceding cards. There are always at least $pn$ available positions. Cauchy–Schwarz bounds its expected conditional variation distance by $\frac12\sqrt{n\kappa_d^R}$. Conditioning on the preceding endpoints alone can only decrease this expectation: the uniform reference on available positions is already measurable from those endpoints, and the conditional law is the conditional expectation of the path-conditioned law. Finally interpolate between joint laws with a true prefix of length $j$ and uniform sampling without replacement thereafter. Consecutive laws differ by the conditional error at the next card, averaged under the actual prefix law. Summing at most $n$ such errors proves the bound. ◻

</details>

<a id="cycles:coarse"></a>
#### Coarse averaging and the energy of a second sweep

We first give an independent noise-based argument. It controls coarse block averages by a martingale expansion, then uses the remaining coordinates of a second sweep to remove energy. The following subsection will obtain sharper block moments from the transverse fibers instead.

<a id="stmt-cycles-coarse-prop"></a>
<div id="cycles:coarse-prop" class="proposition">

<a id="cycles:coarse-contraction"></a>
**Proposition 22** (Coarse-energy contraction). *For $|F|\ge n/8$ and $\sum_xf(x)=0$, the signed-weight process satisfies, for all sufficiently large $d$, $$\label{cycles:coarse-contraction}
 \mathbb E\|f_{2d}\|_2^2\le n^{-1/256}\|f_0\|_2^2.$$ Consequently $4096$ sweeps mix every fixed list of at most $7n/8$ cards with variation error at most $\frac12 n^{-5/2}$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-cycles-coarse-prop"><summary>Proof of stmt-cycles-coarse-prop</summary>

<a id="cycles:coarse-moments"></a>
*Proof.* Let $m=\lfloor3d/4\rfloor$ and $p=|F_0|/n$. At layer $j$ of a sweep, $$f_j=A_jf_{j-1}+\xi_j.$$ Conditional on the past, $\xi_j$ is the sum, over pairs $\{u,v\}$ with exactly one available endpoint $u$, of independent centered vectors $\pm f_{j-1}(u)(e_u-e_v)/2$. Here $e_x$ denotes the unit vector at a position $x$. Expanding the entire sweep, the centered noise terms at different times are orthogonal in second moment, even after applying deterministic averaging operators. Moreover $\|B_m(e_u-e_v)\|_2^2\le2\cdot2^{-m}$, and all coordinate averages commute. Since $B_df_0=0$, and writing $f^*,h^*$ for the output, $$\label{cycles:coarse-moments}
 \mathbb E\|B_mf^*\|_2^2\le d2^{-m}\|f_0\|_2^2,\qquad
 \mathbb E\|B_mh^*-p\mathbf 1\|_2^2\le d2^{-m}n.$$ For the second inequality use the same expansion for flags and $\|h_0\|_2^2=pn\le n$. Energy monotonicity bounds each layer’s sum of squared noise coefficients by the initial energy.

A level-$m$ block varies in coordinates $1,\ldots,m$. If one such block has a fraction of available positions below $1/16$, the second squared norm in <a href="#cycles:coarse-moments" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="cycles:coarse-moments">[cycles:coarse-moments]</a> is at least $2^m/256$. Thus the event $\mathcal G$ that all these blocks have density at least $1/16$ satisfies $\Pr(\mathcal G^c)\le256dn2^{-2m}$.

Condition on the output of sweep one. Before coordinate $j$ of sweep two, distinct level-$(j-1)$ blocks have used disjoint fresh coins. In particular the two endpoints $x,y$ of the next pair have independent flag-weight data, whose means are the entries of $B_{j-1}h^*,B_{j-1}f^*$. Their energy loss is exactly $$\frac12\bigl(h(y)f(x)^2+h(x)f(y)^2-2f(x)f(y)\bigr).$$ On $\mathcal G$, for $j>m$ both flag means are at least $1/16$. The sum of the expected cross products over the pairs is at most $\frac12\|B_{j-1}f^*\|_2^2\le\frac12\|B_mf^*\|_2^2$. The conditional expected energy therefore contracts by $31/32$ at each such step, with additive term $\frac12\|B_mf^*\|_2^2$. Iterating this recurrence, and using monotonicity on $\mathcal G^c$, gives <a id="cycles:coarse-factor"></a>$$\label{cycles:coarse-factor}
 \mathbb E\|f_{2d}\|_2^2\le
 \left((31/32)^{d-m}+16d2^{-m}+256dn2^{-2m}\right)\|f_0\|_2^2.$$ Each term is $o(n^{-1/256})$: for the first use $(31/32)^{d-m}\le e^{-d/128}$, while the others have powers at least $3/4$ and $1/2$, up to polynomial factors in $d$. This proves <a href="#cycles:coarse-contraction" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="cycles:coarse-contraction">[cycles:coarse-contraction]</a>. Iterating $2048$ two-sweep blocks gives energy $n^{-8}$, and Lemma <a href="#cycles:list" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="cycles:list">21</a> gives the stated marginal error. ◻

</details>

<a id="cycles:block-core"></a>
#### Block statistics and the exact merge

A level-$j$ block fixes coordinates $j+1,\ldots,d$ and varies the first $j$; write $\mathcal B_j$ for this partition into blocks of size $2^j$. Its transverse fibers fix the first $j$ coordinates and vary the rest. The first $j$ layers act inside the blocks. Once those layers are fixed, the remaining layers act independently in the transverse fibers. Writing a site as $(a,b)$, the prefix $a$ indexes the fibers and the suffix $b$ indexes the blocks. Each block meets each fiber once, as in Figure <a href="#cycles:transverse-figure" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="cycles:transverse-figure">1</a>. This crossing of the two partitions gives both a small signed block sum and a concentrated available count at the end of a sweep.

<figure id="cycles:transverse-figure">

<figcaption>The case $d = 4$, $k = 2$. The first $k$ layers act within the horizontal blocks. After those layers are fixed, the remaining layers evolve independently in the vertical fibers. Each horizontal block receives one final site from every fiber.</figcaption>
</figure>
